scenario: Contoso has offices in Toronto and Vancouver in a single Entra ID tenant. The Toronto helpdesk must be able to reset passwords and edit user properties for Toronto staff only. They must not be able to touch Vancouver accounts.
options: Create an administrative unit containing the Toronto users, then assign a role scoped to that administrative unit
Assign the Toronto helpdesk the Global Administrator role and rely on written policy
Create a dynamic security group of Toronto users and assign the helpdesk as group owners
Create a second Entra ID tenant for the Toronto office
explain: Administrative units delegate admin permissions over a subset of the directory. The four steps are: create the AU, populate it with users or groups, create a role scoped to the AU, then add IT members to that role. AUs require Entra ID P1 or P2, and you need Privileged Role Administrator or Global Administrator to create one. Group ownership does not grant password-reset rights, and Global Administrator is tenant-wide.

scenario: You open a user account in the Entra admin center. The Source field reads Windows Server AD. The user has just been promoted and their job title needs updating.
q: Where must the change be made?
options: In on-premises Active Directory, so it syncs up through Entra Connect
Directly in the Entra ID portal; the change syncs down to on-premises AD
In either location, since Entra Connect performs two-way synchronization by default
In the Azure subscription properties for that user
explain: A Source of Windows Server AD means this is a directory-synchronized identity. Entra Connect synchronizes from on-premises AD into Entra ID, so the on-premises directory is authoritative for these attributes. The other two source values you should recognize are Azure Active Directory (a cloud identity) and Invited user (a guest).

scenario: Security wants to automatically block sign-ins that Entra ID assesses as high risk, based on signals like impossible travel and leaked credentials. Budget approval requires you to name the minimum license.
q: Which Entra ID plan is the minimum that supports this?
options: Entra ID P2
Entra ID P1
Entra ID Free
Any plan, if MFA is enabled
explain: Risk-based Conditional Access (sign-in risk and user risk) is a P2 feature, as is Privileged Identity Management and governance. P1 gives you plain Conditional Access, advanced group management, automated provisioning to apps, and administrative units. Free covers unlimited SSO, cloud and federated authentication, the self-service account management portal, and MFA.

scenario: As laptops are enrolled, they must automatically join a group used to target a compliance policy. No administrator should have to add them manually.
q: What group type and membership type do you create?
options: A security group with Dynamic Device membership
A Microsoft 365 group with Dynamic Device membership
A security group with Assigned membership
A Microsoft 365 group with Dynamic User membership
explain: Dynamic Device membership is available only for security groups, not Microsoft 365 groups. The three membership types are Assigned, Dynamic User, and Dynamic Device, and only the last is restricted by group type. This is a favourite exam distinction.

scenario: An external design agency needs access to a SharePoint site in your tenant. You invite one of their staff using their existing work email address.
q: What will the Source field show for the new account?
options: Invited user
Windows Server AD
Azure Active Directory
External Identity Provider
explain: Guest users exist outside Azure, such as accounts from other cloud providers or other organizations, and their source is shown as Invited user. Cloud identities show Azure Active Directory; synchronized identities show Windows Server AD.

scenario: Helpdesk volume is dominated by password resets. You are enabling self-service password reset and want users to be challenged by two separate factors before a reset succeeds.
options: The number of authentication methods required
Whether users are required to register for SSPR
Which users are in scope for SSPR
The password writeback setting in Entra Connect
explain: SSPR configuration has three decisions: determine who can use it, choose the number of authentication methods required and which methods are available (email, phone, questions), and decide whether to require users to register (the same process as MFA registration).

scenario: A developer asks why they cannot apply a Group Policy Object to a group of cloud-only users in Entra ID.
options: Entra ID users and groups are created in a flat structure with no OUs or GPOs
GPOs require the Entra ID P2 license, which the tenant does not have
GPOs can only be applied to devices, never to users
Entra Connect must be installed before GPOs can be applied to cloud users
explain: Entra ID is primarily an identity solution with a flat structure: there are no organizational units and no Group Policy Objects. Device configuration in the cloud is handled by Intune compliance and configuration policies instead. AD DS is the hierarchical directory with OUs, GPOs, domains, and forests.

scenario: You are scripting the creation of a Developers group and need to add a user to it from Azure Cloud Shell.
options: Add-AzADGroupMember
New-AzADGroupMember
Set-AzADGroup -AddMember
Add-AzRoleAssignment
explain: The sequence is New-AzADGroup to create, Get-AzADGroup and Get-AzADUser to retrieve object IDs, Add-AzADGroupMember to add the user, and Get-AzADGroupMember to verify. Add-AzRoleAssignment grants RBAC permissions, which is a different operation.

scenario: A project team needs a shared mailbox, a shared calendar, and a shared document library, all provisioned from one group object.
q: Which group type do you create?
options: A Microsoft 365 group
A security group
A distribution list in on-premises Exchange
An administrative unit
explain: Microsoft 365 groups are the collaboration group type and provision a mailbox, calendar, and files. Security groups manage access to resources but bring no collaboration workload with them.

scenario: Contoso acquires Fabrikam. Leadership wants one identity for all staff so people sign in once, but the two divisions must be billed separately and their resources kept in separate management boundaries.
q: Explain how tenants and subscriptions let you satisfy both requirements, and define each term.
model: A tenant (directory) is a dedicated, trusted instance of Microsoft Entra ID representing a single organization. It is the identity boundary, is created automatically when the organization signs up for a Microsoft cloud service, and holds the users and groups. An Azure subscription is a logical container used to provision and manage Azure resources, and it is the unit of management, billing, and scale that pays for Azure services. Because one tenant can trust many subscriptions, Contoso keeps a single tenant so every user has one identity and gets single sign-on, and then creates two subscriptions, one per division, so each division has its own billing unit and its own management and scale boundary. Resources cannot span subscriptions, so the separation is enforced structurally.

scenario: Your organization runs Windows Server AD on-premises and wants users to reach Entra ID-managed SaaS apps without extra authentication prompts, even when their laptops are off the corporate network.
q: Which benefit of Entra ID and on-premises AD join describes this?
options: Single Sign-On
Enterprise compliant roaming
Seamless on-premises resource access
Compliance policy enforcement
explain: Single Sign-On lets users access Entra ID-managed SaaS apps and services without additional authentication prompts even when not connected to the domain network. Seamless on-premises resource access is the opposite direction and requires line of sight to a domain controller. Enterprise compliant roaming is about user settings following the user across joined devices.

scenario: An architect asks which component actually performs the synchronization between your on-premises Windows Server AD and Entra ID.
options: Microsoft Entra Connect
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Azure AD Application Proxy
The Azure Backup MARS agent
explain: Entra Connect performs the directory synchronization. Entra Domain Services is a separate managed service that provides domain join, LDAP, and Kerberos in Azure without you deploying domain controllers.

scenario: Finance wants to charge cloud spend back by department. You apply the tag CostCenter=Marketing to the marketing resource group, which contains 14 virtual machines. A week later the cost report shows no tagged VM spend.
options: Tags applied to a resource group are not inherited by the resources inside it
Cost analysis only reports tags applied at the subscription level
The resource group exceeded the 50-tag limit
Tags take 30 days to appear in Cost Management
explain: This is one of the most commonly tested facts in the course: tags applied to a resource group are not inherited by the resources in that resource group. To bill back by tag you must tag the resources themselves, typically enforced with Azure Policy. Each resource or resource group can carry a maximum of 50 tag name/value pairs.

scenario: A production resource group must be protected from accidental deletion, but the operations team still needs to resize VMs and change configuration inside it.
options: A Delete (CanNotDelete) lock on the resource group
A ReadOnly lock on the resource group
A ReadOnly lock on each virtual machine
A Delete lock on the subscription
explain: A Delete lock prevents deletion while still allowing changes. A ReadOnly lock prevents any changes at all, which would block the resizing the team needs. Locks can be applied at subscription, resource group, or resource scope and are inherited by child resources.

scenario: A Contributor on the subscription reports that they cannot remove a management lock that is blocking their work.
q: Which roles can create or delete management locks?
options: Owner and User Access Administrator
Owner and Contributor
Contributor and Reader
Any role with write permission on the resource
explain: Only the Owner and User Access Administrator roles can create or delete management locks. Contributor can create and manage all resources but cannot grant access, and lock management is treated as an access operation.

scenario: A new junior administrator must be able to create, modify, and delete virtual machines in the Dev resource group, but must never be able to give anyone else permissions.
q: Which built-in role do you assign, and at what scope?
options: Contributor, scoped to the Dev resource group
Owner, scoped to the Dev resource group
User Access Administrator, scoped to the Dev resource group
Contributor, scoped to the subscription
explain: Contributor can create and manage all resources but cannot grant access to others, which is exactly the requirement. Owner adds the ability to delegate access. Scope it at the resource group so the permission does not extend to the rest of the subscription, since resources inherit role assignments from their parent.

scenario: Compliance requires that no resource may be deployed outside Canada Central and Canada East, regardless of who is deploying.
options: An Azure Policy restricting allowed locations
An RBAC role assignment limited to those regions
A ReadOnly lock on all other regions
A resource tag named AllowedRegion
explain: Azure Policy enforces organizational standards and compliance: what may be deployed and with what settings. RBAC governs who can deploy, not where. Tags label resources but enforce nothing on their own.

scenario: You assign the Reader role to an auditor at the subscription scope.
q: What access does the auditor have to a resource group created later inside that subscription?
options: Read access, because resources inherit role assignments from their parent
No access, because the assignment predates the resource group
Read access only if the assignment is repeated at the resource group scope
Full access, because subscription-level assignments always elevate
explain: A role assignment binds a role to a security principal at a particular scope, and a resource inherits role assignments from its parent resources. The scope hierarchy flows management group, subscription, resource group, resource, and inheritance runs downward, including to resources created afterwards.

scenario: Your organization signs an Enterprise Agreement and makes an upfront monetary commitment that is consumed across Azure services during the year. The service desk asks what monthly SLA the agreement carries.
explain: Enterprise agreements carry a 99.95% monthly SLA. The other subscription routes covered in the module are reseller (Open Licensing), partners, and the personal free account, which is not charged until you choose to upgrade.

scenario: The CFO wants to be notified automatically when the Dev subscription passes 80 percent of its planned monthly spend.
q: Which Cost Management feature do you use?
options: Budgets
Cost analysis
Recommendations
Exporting cost management data
explain: Budgets set spending thresholds with alerts. Cost analysis is for exploring and analyzing spend after the fact, Recommendations advise on reducing cost, and export pushes data out for external reporting.

scenario: An architect asks why Azure replicates geo-redundant storage to one specific other region rather than any region you choose.
options: Each Azure region is paired with another region within the same geography, forming a regional pair
Azure replicates to whichever region currently has the most free capacity
Replication always targets the region alphabetically closest in name
Regional pairing is configured per storage account at creation
explain: A region is a geographical area containing at least one, and potentially multiple, datacenters. Each region is paired with another within the same geography. Pairing keeps replicated data inside the same geography for residency, and platform updates roll out to only one region of a pair at a time.

scenario: A team lead argues that because their developers already hold the Contributor role, there is no need for the new Azure Policy that blocks expensive VM SKUs.
q: Explain the difference between what RBAC controls and what Azure Policy controls, and why both are needed here.
model: RBAC governs who can perform actions on Azure resources: a role assignment binds a role to a security principal at a particular scope, granting access, and resources inherit role assignments from their parent. Contributor lets the developers create and manage all resources but not grant access to others. Azure Policy governs what may be deployed and with what settings, enforcing organizational standards and compliance, for example allowed VM SKUs, required tags, or permitted regions. The two are complementary: RBAC says the developers are allowed to create virtual machines at all, and Policy constrains which virtual machines they are allowed to create. Without the policy, the Contributor role by itself permits any SKU in the subscription.

scenario: You are documenting the difference between Azure RBAC roles and Entra ID roles for a new hire.
options: Azure RBAC roles control access to Azure resources and can be scoped to a resource group; Entra ID roles control access to Entra ID resources and are tenant-wide
Both role systems are scoped identically and the names are interchangeable
Entra ID roles can be scoped to a single virtual machine
Azure RBAC roles are tenant-wide and Entra ID roles are resource-scoped
explain: Azure RBAC roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator) apply to Azure resources at management group, subscription, resource group, or resource scope. Entra ID roles (Global Administrator, User Administrator, Billing Administrator) apply to directory objects such as users, groups, licenses, and domains, and are tenant-wide.

scenario: You must deploy an identical virtual network with the same three subnets into Dev, Test, and Prod, and be able to redeploy any of them from scratch after a failure.
options: Author an ARM template and deploy it three times with different parameters
Create the first VNet in the portal and manually recreate it twice
Script the portal clicks with a browser automation tool
Create one VNet and move it between resource groups as needed
explain: An ARM template is a JSON file that declaratively defines one or more resources to deploy to a resource group. Declarative syntax means you define the properties of the infrastructure you want without writing programming commands to create it, which gives you repeatable, version-controlled, parameterized deployments.

scenario: You are editing an exported ARM template so that the administrator username and password are supplied at deployment time rather than hard-coded.
q: Which template section do these values belong in?
options: parameters
variables
resources
outputs
explain: The parameters section specifies which values you can input when deploying the resources; the classic example is a virtual machine username and password. Variables hold values reused inside the template, resources holds what actually gets deployed, and outputs returns values after deployment.

scenario: After a corporate rebrand you are asked to rename the resource group rg-oldname to rg-newname, keeping all 30 resources in place.
q: What do you tell the requester?
options: Resource groups cannot be renamed; you must create a new one and move the resources
Rename it from the Overview blade; the change is instant
Rename it with Set-AzResourceGroup -NewName
Rename it, but only if no resource has a lock
explain: Resource groups cannot be renamed. The workaround is to create the new group and move resources into it. Note that during a move both the source and target resource groups are locked: write and delete operations are blocked on both until the move completes, although the resources themselves stay available.

scenario: A move of 12 resources between resource groups is in progress. A colleague messages to ask whether the web app being moved is currently down.
options: No. Both resource groups are locked against write and delete operations, but the resources remain available
Yes. Moved resources are offline until the operation completes
Yes, but only resources in the target resource group are offline
No, and you can also add new resources to both groups during the move
explain: When moving resources, both the source group and the target group are locked during the operation. Write and delete operations are blocked, so you cannot add, update, or delete resources in either group, but the lock does not mean the resources are unavailable.

scenario: A colleague opens Cloud Shell for the first time and is prompted to create supporting resources before the shell will start.
options: A resource group, a storage account, and an Azure File share
A virtual machine and a public IP address
A virtual network with a dedicated subnet
An App Service plan
explain: Cloud Shell is an interactive, browser-accessible shell that authenticates automatically. It requires a resource group, a storage account, and an Azure File share, and it persists your $HOME directory using a 5-GB image held in that file share. Bash and PowerShell are both available.

scenario: You need to delete a large resource group from Cloud Shell but do not want the console to block while it runs.
options: Remove-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-legacy" -Force -AsJob
Remove-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-legacy" -Wait
Delete-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-legacy"
Remove-AzResource -ResourceGroupName "rg-legacy" -Recurse
explain: Remove-AzResourceGroup deletes the group; -Force suppresses the confirmation prompt and -AsJob runs it in the background so the shell returns immediately. Get-AzResourceGroup lists groups. Azure PowerShell always follows the Verb-AzNoun pattern.

scenario: A deployment fails because your subscription has hit the documented maximum limit for a resource type, not the default limit.
options: Nothing can be done for that subscription; when you are at the maximum limit it cannot be increased
Use the Request Increase link to raise it beyond the maximum
Open a support ticket to have the maximum waived
Move the resources to another region, which resets the maximum
explain: The limits shown are the limits for your subscription. Where a default limit applies there is a Request Increase link, but all resources also have a maximum limit listed in Azure limits, and if you are at the maximum it cannot be increased. The practical answer in that case is a second subscription.

scenario: You are explaining what happens between clicking Create in the portal and the virtual machine appearing.
options: The tool calls the ARM API, ARM authenticates and authorizes the request, then routes it to the appropriate resource provider
The portal writes directly to the datacenter fabric, bypassing ARM for speed
The request goes to the resource provider first, which then calls ARM for authorization
PowerShell and CLI bypass ARM; only the portal uses it
explain: All Azure tools interact with the Azure Resource Manager API. ARM authenticates and authorizes the request and then routes it to the appropriate resource provider, for example Microsoft.Compute for virtual machines, Microsoft.Storage for storage accounts, or Microsoft.Web for web apps. This is why RBAC, tagging, and locks behave identically no matter which tool you use.

scenario: An audit asks which resource provider supplies the virtual machine resource type.
options: Microsoft.Compute
Microsoft.Storage
Microsoft.Web
Microsoft.Network
explain: Microsoft.Compute supplies the VM resource, Microsoft.Storage supplies the storage account resource, and Microsoft.Web supplies resources related to web apps.

scenario: A team proposes putting a production database, a short-lived test VM, and a shared corporate DNS server in the same resource group for convenience.
q: What is the design principle they are violating?
options: All resources in a group should share the same lifecycle: you deploy, update, and delete them together
A resource group may only contain one resource type
A resource group may only contain resources from a single region
A resource group may hold no more than 50 resources
explain: A resource group is a logical container for related resources, and all resources in the group should share the same lifecycle. Resource groups can freely span types and regions, and a resource can only exist in one resource group. Grouping items with different lifecycles makes deletion and redeployment dangerous.

scenario: You place a ReadOnly lock on a storage account, then attempt to delete it.
options: The deletion is blocked, because a ReadOnly lock prevents any changes to the resource
The deletion succeeds, because ReadOnly only blocks configuration edits
The deletion succeeds after a warning prompt
The deletion is blocked only if a Delete lock also exists
explain: There are two lock types: ReadOnly, which prevents any changes to the resource, and Delete, which prevents deletion. ReadOnly is the stricter of the two and blocks deletion as well as modification.

scenario: You build the CoreServicesVnet in the portal, export it as a template, edit template.json and parameters.json, and redeploy it as a second network, the ManufacturingVnet.
q: Explain why exporting and editing a template is preferable to building the second VNet by hand in the portal.
model: The exported ARM template is a JSON file that declaratively defines the resources, so it captures the exact configuration of the working CoreServicesVnet including address space, subnets, and their properties. Redeploying it guarantees the second network is structurally identical rather than depending on an administrator repeating every portal click correctly, which removes configuration drift and human error. Because the values that change between environments live in parameters, the same template can be reused for many deployments, kept in version control, reviewed, and redeployed to rebuild the environment after a failure. Deployment is also faster and repeatable or idempotent, and the template documents the infrastructure.

scenario: You size a subnet as 10.20.30.0/27 for a small application tier and plan to place 30 virtual machines in it.
q: How many virtual machines can actually be addressed?
explain: Azure reserves five IP addresses in every subnet: x.0 as the network address, x.1 for the Azure default gateway, x.2 and x.3 to map the Azure DNS IPs into the VNet space, and the last address as the network broadcast address. A /27 has 32 addresses, so 32 minus 5 leaves 27 usable.

scenario: A VM cannot be reached on port 443 from another subnet. You check the NIC NSG and find an inbound rule at priority 300 that allows TCP 443 from any source. The subnet NSG contains a rule at priority 200 that denies TCP 443.
q: Why is traffic still blocked, and where is it blocked?
options: NSGs are evaluated independently and an allow rule must exist at both levels; the subnet NSG is evaluated first for inbound traffic and denies it
The NIC rule should win because it is more specific to the VM
The rules cancel out and traffic is allowed by the default VirtualNetwork rule
The NIC NSG priority 300 is higher than 200, so it overrides the subnet rule
explain: NSGs are evaluated independently and an allow rule must exist at both levels for traffic to pass. For incoming traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; for outgoing traffic it is the reverse. Also note that lower priority numbers are evaluated first, so 200 beats 300 within a single NSG. Use the Effective security rules view to see the combined result.

scenario: An NSG contains a rule at priority 150 denying TCP 3389 from any source, and a rule at priority 400 allowing TCP 3389 from your office IP range.
q: Can you RDP from the office?
options: No. Rules are processed in priority order and the lower number wins, so the deny at 150 matches first
Yes. Allow rules always take precedence over deny rules
Yes. The more specific source range makes the allow rule win
It depends on whether the NSG is attached to the subnet or the NIC
explain: Rules are processed in priority order and the lower the number, the higher the priority. Processing stops at the first match, so the deny at 150 wins. To fix it, give the allow rule a number lower than 150. Custom rules use the range 100 to 4096.

scenario: Your web tier scales up and down constantly. Security rules must permit the web VMs to reach the database VMs on port 1433, but you refuse to maintain a list of IP addresses that changes every day.
options: Application security groups referenced as the source and destination in the NSG rule
A single NSG rule using the VirtualNetwork service tag on both sides
A user-defined route between the two subnets
An Azure Firewall network rule listing each VM IP
explain: An application security group is a logical grouping of network interfaces by application role. It contains no rules itself; you reference it as the source or destination inside an NSG rule, so membership changes automatically apply and no IP addresses need to be maintained. The VirtualNetwork service tag would be far too broad, permitting every VM in the network.

scenario: A server administrator sets a static IP address inside the guest operating system of an Azure VM to match the private IP shown in the portal. The VM immediately loses network connectivity.
options: IP addresses are never managed from within a virtual machine; they must be configured in Azure
The static address must be one number higher than the portal value
The VM needed a reboot for the guest OS change to register with Azure
Static addresses are only permitted on Standard SKU public IPs
explain: IP addresses are never managed from within a virtual machine. Assign addresses in Azure, choosing static or dynamic (DHCP) on the NIC. It is also good practice to separate dynamically and statically assigned resources into different subnets.

scenario: Virtual machines behind Azure Firewall must be able to reach *.windowsupdate.com over HTTPS, and nothing else on the internet.
q: Which rule type do you create?
options: An application rule, which defines the FQDNs that can be accessed from a subnet
A network rule specifying TCP 443 to any destination
A NAT rule translating port 443 to the update servers
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Update
explain: Application rules define fully qualified domain names that can be accessed from a subnet, support wildcards, and support FQDN tags representing groups of FQDNs for well-known Microsoft services such as Windows Update, App Service Environment, and Azure Backup. Network rules filter by IP, port, and protocol and cannot match on domain name.

scenario: You need to publish an internal web server, which has only a private IP, to the internet through the public IP of your Azure Firewall.
options: A NAT (DNAT) rule, which must also be matched by a network rule to allow traffic to pass
An application rule listing the server FQDN
A network rule alone, since NAT is automatic for inbound traffic
A user-defined route with the firewall as next hop, and nothing else
explain: Azure Firewall DNAT translates and filters inbound traffic to Azure subnets, translating the firewall public IP and port to a private IP and port. The NAT rule must be matched by a network rule to allow the traffic through. Its settings include source address, destination address (the firewall external address), destination ports, translated address, and translated port.

scenario: Azure Firewall has just been deployed in front of a subnet and no rules have been created. Users report that nothing works.
options: Yes. By default Azure Firewall blocks all traffic until rules are created
No. Azure Firewall allows all outbound traffic by default
No. Azure Firewall inherits the NSG rules of the subnet it protects
Yes, but only for inbound traffic; outbound is open by default
explain: By default Azure Firewall blocks all traffic. Rules are processed in the order NAT, then network, then application, and once a rule is found that allows the traffic through, no more rules are checked.

scenario: You add contoso.ca as a custom domain in your Entra ID tenant. It shows as unverified.
q: Which DNS record type can you add to verify ownership?
options: MX or TXT
A or AAAA
CNAME or SRV
NS or SOA
explain: Verification is performed by adding a DNS record, which can be an MX or TXT record. Once Azure verifies the record it adds the domain name to the subscription. Only one directory can use a domain name: the organization that owns it. Note the contrast with mapping a custom domain to a web app, which uses a CNAME or A record.

scenario: You create a private DNS zone named private.contoso.ca and add an A record for a VM, but no virtual machine can resolve the name.
options: A virtual network link from the private DNS zone to each VNet that needs private name resolution
A set of name server records, which private zones create automatically once populated
A public DNS zone with the same name to delegate from
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Network on the subnet
explain: A private DNS zone is only accessible from the virtual networks it is linked to and cannot be reached from the internet. You must add a virtual network link for each VNet needing resolution. Private zones have no name server records, which is the visible difference from a public zone on the Overview blade.

scenario: Two different teams each create a DNS zone named contoso.ca, in two different resource groups in the same subscription.
options: Both are created successfully, and each instance is assigned different name server addresses
The second creation fails because zone names must be globally unique
The second zone silently overwrites the first
Both are created and share the same name servers
explain: The name of the zone must be unique within the resource group, and the same zone name can be reused in a different resource group. Where multiple zones share the same name, each instance is assigned different name server addresses, so only the zone whose name servers the registrar points to is authoritative.

scenario: You are asked how many network security groups can be attached to a single subnet.
options: Zero or one
Exactly one, always
Up to five
Unlimited, evaluated in priority order
explain: You can associate zero or one network security group to each subnet, and the same is true for each network interface. A single NSG can, however, be associated many times across different subnets and NICs, which is how you reuse one rule set.

scenario: Reviewing the outbound rules of a new NSG, you find AllowInternetOutbound at priority 65001, which cannot be deleted. You need to block outbound access to the internet on TCP 8080.
options: Add a custom deny rule with a priority number lower than 65001, using the Internet service tag as the destination
Delete the default rule and recreate it as a deny
Raise the default rule priority above 65001
Apply the deny rule to the NIC instead, since defaults only apply to subnets
explain: Default rules cannot be deleted, but any custom rule with a lower priority number is evaluated first and therefore overrides them. A deny rule for this would use destination Service tag Internet, port 8080, action Deny, priority 4096. Custom priorities run from 100 to 4096, all of which are below the 65000-range defaults.

scenario: A new subnet must be created but the only unallocated space left in the VNet is a /29.
q: How many usable IP addresses will that subnet provide?
explain: A /29 contains 8 addresses and Azure reserves five in every subnet, leaving 3 usable. This is why the module stresses planning for service requirements: some services require their own subnet, so you need enough unallocated address space.

scenario: Your subscription already has 50 virtual networks in East US and a new project needs more.
options: 50 per subscription per region is the default limit and it can be raised to 500 by contacting Azure support
50 is the hard maximum and cannot be raised
The limit is per subscription overall, so deploying in another region will not help
You must create a second subscription; VNet limits cannot be increased
explain: By default you can create up to 50 virtual networks per subscription per region, and this limit can be increased to 500 by contacting Azure support. Note the limit is per region, so another region gets its own allowance.

scenario: You want a single Azure Firewall to enforce and log rules for workloads that live in several different subscriptions and virtual networks.
options: Yes. Azure Firewall network filtering rules are enforced and logged across multiple subscriptions and virtual networks
No. A firewall instance is limited to the virtual network it is deployed in
Yes, but only if all virtual networks are in the same resource group
No. Cross-subscription enforcement requires one firewall per subscription
explain: Azure Firewall is fully stateful and its rules are enforced and logged across multiple subscriptions and virtual networks. Other features include built-in high availability with no extra load balancers, availability zone support, unrestricted cloud scalability, FQDN filtering, threat intelligence based filtering from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence feed, and up to 100 associated public IP addresses.

scenario: A colleague has created an NSG rule allowing TCP 443 inbound on the NIC of a web server, but external traffic still does not reach it. The subnet the NIC lives in also has an NSG attached.
q: Describe how you would troubleshoot this, naming the evaluation order and the tools you would use.
model: NSGs are evaluated independently and an allow rule must exist at both levels for traffic to pass. For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first and then the NIC NSG, so even a correct NIC rule is useless if the subnet NSG denies the traffic. Within each NSG, rules are processed in priority order and the lower the number, the higher the priority, with processing stopping at the first match, so a low-numbered deny can shadow a higher-numbered allow. I would open the Effective security rules view on the network interface to see the combined result of both NSGs, and use Network Watcher IP Flow Verify to confirm whether the packet is allowed or denied and which rule is responsible. If the packet is allowed but still not arriving, I would then check routing with Next Hop and end-to-end reachability with Connection Troubleshoot.

scenario: You are documenting DNS terminology and need to define a record set.
